summary: A discussion of the Pcmail workstation-based distributed mail system, identical to RFC 993 except for a new, much simpler mail transport protocol. That change came from continued research into making protocols easier to implement and use. It replaces RFC 993.

plainLanguage.summary: Pcmail keeps a central copy of each user's mail and lets several computers keep their own copies. Its protocol synchronizes changes when a computer connects to the repository.

questions: how does the pcmail transport protocol work
subtitle: A distributed mail system with local copies and a simple synchronization protocol.

tldr.problem: Users may have several workstations, including small computers that connect only sometimes, but still need consistent access to their mail.
tldr.mechanism: A repository stores each user's global mail state. Clients keep local copies and synchronize them using DMSP, a request-and-response protocol over a reliable byte stream.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1056 repeats the system discussion in RFC 993 but replaces its transport protocol with a simpler one. It obsoletes RFC 993 and is Informational.

today: RFC 1056 is an Informational RFC published in June 1988. It obsoletes RFC 993; the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: A Repository and Multiple Clients
sections.content:
Pcmail serves users who may own one or more workstations. A repository stores incoming mail and the global mail state. Each client keeps a local copy so the user can work when the network is unavailable.

Because local and global copies can change separately, the system needs synchronization. The RFC says it is the same system discussion as RFC 993, except that this version describes a new and simpler mail transport protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The repository is the central store for mail, and each client keeps a local copy. When a client reconnects, it synchronizes its copy with the repository.

sections.title: Mail Objects and Message Summaries
sections.content:
The repository organizes users, client records, mailboxes, subscriptions, addresses, and messages. A message has a descriptor with its UID, size, selected header fields, and flags, plus a body containing the message.

A descriptor is typically about 100 bytes regardless of the message size. A client with limited storage can keep descriptors for its messages and fetch or print a body when needed. The repository also keeps an update list for each client so it can report changes since the last synchronization.
sections.plainLanguage: A message has a small summary and a separate body. A computer with little storage can keep summaries and request full messages later.

sections.title: DMSP Requests and Replies
sections.content:
The Distributed Mail System Protocol (DMSP) runs on a reliable bidirectional byte stream, such as TCP. Its contact port is 158. A request contains an operation name and arguments on a line; the repository returns a three-digit code and may return a list of lines ending with a period on its own line.

The first reply digit indicates an informative response, success, success with more text, failure, or a syntax error. A session begins with login and ends with logout. Each operation is failure-atomic: without an explicit success acknowledgement, the operation is considered failed and mail state remains consistent.
sections.plainLanguage: A client sends a command line and gets a numbered reply. An operation counts as successful only when the repository confirms it.

sections.title: Synchronizing Local and Global Mail
sections.content:
In interactive mode, client changes are sent to the repository at once. In batch mode, the client records changes locally and sends them the next time it connects. It then retrieves new mail and changes made by other clients.

The repository returns changed descriptors and expunged-message notices. After storing those changes locally, the client tells the repository which UID range it recorded. This lets the repository avoid sending the same changes again unless they change later.
sections.plainLanguage: When a client reconnects, it asks what changed, updates its local copy, and confirms which changes it recorded. Batch clients send their own queued changes before synchronizing.

sections.title: Implementation and Security Limits
sections.content:
The RFC describes a Pcmail implementation used by a small community at MIT's Laboratory for Computer Science. Its IBM PC clients used batch mode, while its UNIX clients supported interactive operation. The implementation report says performance was good with up to ten connected users.

DMSP sends passwords in clear text because encryption was considered difficult for resource-limited clients; the RFC calls this unacceptable as a long-term solution. It also relies on the repository's availability and uses locking to prevent concurrent clients from modifying the same mail state at once.
sections.plainLanguage: The described system was used by a small group and had different client modes for different computers. Its password transfer was not protected, which the RFC identified as a problem.

references.text: Lambert, M., "PCMAIL: A distributed mail system for personal computers", RFC 993, February 1986.
